headline: 🔥 PLAGUE-RUMOR CATCHES FIRE IN THE FORUM
factoid: Procopius records that during the 542 CE Plague of Justinian, Constantinople was flooded with rumors blaming imperial taxation, foreign agents, and minority communities for the outbreak. Rumor as a tool for redirecting collective panic predates written history.

headline: 🔥 SENATOR'S MISTRESS NAMED IN ANONYMOUS SCROLL
factoid: Pompeii's preserved election graffiti includes coordinated attacks on candidates' fictional indiscretions — 'all the late drinkers ask for Marcus,' 'all the rascals support Vatia.' Roman political smear via graffiti was a documented organised practice.

headline: 🔥 AUGUR REPORTS DARK OMEN OVER RIVAL'S HOUSE
factoid: Roman augury (interpretation of bird flight, lightning, and animal entrails) was officially required before major state decisions. Senators routinely paid favorable augurs to delay or void political opponents' acts — Cicero's writings discuss the practice openly.

headline: 🔥 GRAIN MERCHANTS WHISPER OF NEW TAX
factoid: Salt taxes in late Roman Egypt provoked the 'Bucolic Revolt' of 172 CE; contemporary accounts describe grain merchants spreading rumors of upcoming additional taxes to drive panic-buying. The Roman tax system was a perpetual rumor mill from the early empire onward.

headline: 🔥 LIGHTNING STRUCK THE TEMPLE — GODS DISPLEASED?
factoid: Roman augurs could halt public business by declaring a lightning strike a bad omen. In 59 BCE, Caesar's co-consul Bibulus tried to use this technique to obstruct Caesar's legislation; Caesar simply ignored him and the laws passed.

headline: ⚡ FRENZY: AGORA IN UPROAR — EVERY VOICE CARRIES A LIE
factoid: Aristophanes' The Acharnians (425 BCE) opens with the agora consumed by competing rumor-mongers shouting over each other for the audience's attention. Crowd-driven rumor cascades in ancient agoras are the documented ancestor of every news rush since.
